title: Parts of a baseplate compass
def: A baseplate compass has a clear base with a direction-of-travel arrow, a rotating housing marked in degrees with an orienting arrow and lines, and a magnetic needle whose red end points to magnetic north.
look: the red end of the needle
the degree ring on the housing
a declination adjustment on better models
use: Learn which arrow is which at home: you set bearings with the housing and walk where the direction-of-travel arrow points.
not: Do not store a compass next to magnets or speakers, which can weaken or reverse the needle.

title: Navigating at night
def: Moving at night is slower and riskier; it works only on a known trail or a sure handrail with a good light and a careful bearing.
look: a bright headlamp and spare batteries
a trail, road, or stream edge to follow
landmarks you can find by light
use: Shorten legs between landmarks, count paces, check the compass often, and stop and camp if the ground gets rough.
not: Do not travel cross-country at night in steep or unknown terrain if you can safely wait for light.

title: Rough direction from the sun
def: The sun gives only a rough direction: it rises in the east, sets in the west, and in the northern hemisphere is generally to the south at midday, with big seasonal shifts.
look: a stick's shadow tip moving from west to east over 15-20 minutes
time of day and season
clear enough sky to see shadows
use: Mark a shadow tip, wait 15 minutes, mark again; the line from first to second mark runs roughly west to east. Use it as a check, not a precise bearing.
not: Do not treat sun directions as exact, especially near sunrise, sunset, or in summer when the sun rises well north of east.

title: Stars as a rough north reference
def: In the northern hemisphere the North Star, Polaris, sits almost due north; the two outer stars of the Big Dipper's cup point to it.
look: the Big Dipper's pointer stars
a moderately bright star alone in its area
clear sky away from bright lights
use: Follow the pointer stars about five times their gap to Polaris, then pick a ground landmark below it to hold your direction.
not: Do not use it as a substitute for a compass on long, precise routes.

title: Marking a route for yourself
def: Marking your own route with removable flagging or noted landmarks makes the return trip easier, especially in thick woods or snow.
look: bright, removable flagging tape
waypoints saved only if you chose to
landmarks noted at each turn
use: Tie flagging at eye level where you can see the next one, look back often so you know the return view, and remove the flagging on your way out.
not: Do not cut blazes into trees or leave flagging behind on land where it is not allowed.

title: Whiteout or fog: stay put or follow a sure handrail
def: In fog or a whiteout you lose landmarks and depth; most often the safest choice is to stop, shelter, and wait unless a sure handrail leads you out.
look: no visible landmarks beyond a few yards
snow or fog hiding drop-offs
a trail, fence, or stream you can follow by touch or sight
use: Stop, get warm and sheltered, and wait it out, or follow a known handrail with compass and pace count, staying together.
not: Do not head cross-country toward ridges, cornices, cliffs, or frozen lakes you cannot see.

title: Altimeter or barometer as a rough navigation aid
def: An altimeter estimates your height from air pressure, and matching that height to a contour on the map helps narrow down where you are along a trail or slope.
look: a known elevation to calibrate at the trailhead
weather changes shifting the reading
a contour line that matches your height
use: Calibrate at a known height, recheck at known points, and combine the reading with the trail, stream, or ridge you are on.
not: Do not trust an altimeter alone during a changing storm; pressure swings change the reading.

title: Map scale and what a map does not show
def: A map's scale sets how much detail it can show; a 1:24,000 topographic map shows small streams and contours, while a small-scale map leaves out trails, cliffs, and new roads.
look: the scale and date in the margin
missing new trails, logging roads, or beaver flooding
contour interval size
use: Use the largest-scale map you can get for foot travel and expect changes on the ground since the map's date.
not: Do not assume a map pack shows roads, buildings, or land ownership unless it says so.

title: Driving versus walking when the road is not on the map
def: On unmapped back roads the vehicle is shelter, a big visible target, and a supply cache, so staying with it is often safer than walking out.
look: fuel, weather, and daylight left
distance to the last known road or house
whether anyone knows your route
use: Stay with the vehicle when stuck unless help is close and the way is sure; walking out is safer by daylight on a known road.
not: Do not run the engine for warmth with the exhaust blocked by snow.
call: Call 911 if you have signal; a text may get through when a call will not.

title: Resection and intersection
def: Resection finds your own position by taking bearings to two or three landmarks you can identify on the map and drawing back-bearings; intersection finds a distant point from two known spots.
look: two or three distinct, mapped landmarks far apart in direction
back-bearings: add or subtract 180°
lines crossing in a small triangle
use: Take bearings to the landmarks, convert to back-bearings for the map, draw the lines, and you are near where they cross.
not: Do not use landmarks that are close together in direction; the lines cross at a shallow angle and mislead.

title: Reading grid coordinates on a map
def: Grid coordinates locate a point using the map's grid lines: read the easting (left to right) first, then the northing (bottom to top).
look: the grid line labels along the map edges
a coordinate scale or ruler
the datum and zone printed in the margin
use: Read right, then up; give the coordinates and the datum to rescuers if asked, or read latitude and longitude from your phone.
not: Do not mix up datums or give only partial numbers to rescuers.

title: Turnaround time and trip plans
def: A turnaround time is the hour you turn back no matter where you are, set so you are out before dark or bad weather; a trip plan tells someone your route and return.
look: sunset time and forecast
your pace on the way in
who has your plan
use: Set the turnaround time before you start, keep it, and leave your route and return time with someone who will call for help.
not: Do not push past the turnaround to reach a summit or spot.
